## Provide AI with the mathematics. Then ask it about science.

AI can already reason over mathematics.

R<sup>2</sup>D provides a mathematical interface for converting
scientific objects into a common boundary-dependent representation.

You do not need specialized R<sup>2</sup>D software to begin.

Download the current R<sup>2</sup>D Canon, load it into an AI system
that can work with large documents, provide the R<sup>2</sup>D
instruction below, and then ask AI about a scientific law, paradox,
paper, dataset, or unsolved problem.

[DOWNLOAD THE CURRENT R²D CANON →](https://zenodo.org/records/22760358){target="_blank"}


## 1. Load the Canon

Download the current PDF of the R<sup>2</sup>D Canon from Zenodo and
upload it to the AI system you want to use.  

[DOWNLOAD THE CURRENT R²D CANON →](https://zenodo.org/records/22760358){target="_blank"}

The Canon is the authoritative source. It contains the definitions,
formal architecture, physical mappings, applications, and addenda
needed for the AI to reason within R<sup>2</sup>D rather than
immediately translating the framework back into conventional physical
ontology.


## 2. Give the AI the R<sup>2</sup>D instruction

Copy and paste the following instruction:

> Use the attached R²D Canon as the authoritative source for this analysis.
>
> Work within the definitions and mathematical architecture of R²D before
> translating the problem into conventional physical ontology.
>
> Treat scientific objects, macrostates, microstates, multiplicity,
> possibility, constraint, recurrence, closure, and recursive replacement
> as boundary-dependent quantities as defined in the Canon.
>
> When analyzing the scientific problem I provide:
>
> 1. Identify the scientific object and the boundary at which it is defined.
> 2. Identify which quantities are directly readable at that boundary.
> 3. Separate the empirical mathematical relation from the physical ontology
>    conventionally assigned to it.
> 4. Determine whether the relation can be represented in the R²D
>    architecture without changing the established empirical law.
> 5. Identify any change in state domain produced by changing boundary or scale.
> 6. Distinguish formal deductions from physical mappings, empirical
>    calibrations, hypotheses, and speculation.
> 7. State clearly if the proposed R²D interpretation conflicts with an
>    established scientific result.
>
> Do not assume that R²D is correct. Try to break the mapping.

## 3. Give it a problem

Then ask the question you actually care about.

For example:

> Apply R²D to the Navier–Stokes singularity problem. Strip away the
> inherited spatial ontology where possible, preserve the Navier–Stokes
> mathematics, and determine what changes at the boundary where the
> continuous description fails.

Or:

> Analyze the Einstein field equation using R²D. Separate the empirical
> and geometric content of the equation from assumptions about which
> quantities are primitive.

Or simply:

> Here is a scientific paper. What does R²D see that the conventional
> interpretation does not?


## What to Look For

A useful R<sup>2</sup>D analysis should not merely rename familiar
scientific quantities.

It should expose whether a change of boundary changes the mathematical
state domain, whether a familiar physical object is a projection of a
more primitive count relation, and whether apparently different
scientific descriptions can be deprojected onto the same mathematical
architecture.

Most importantly, it must preserve the empirical science.

If an R<sup>2</sup>D interpretation requires changing an established
law in order to make the framework work, that is evidence against the
interpretation.


## Don't Believe R<sup>2</sup>D. Run It.

R<sup>2</sup>D was developed through repeated attempts to make the
framework fail against established science.

That remains the recommended way to use it.

**Load the Canon. Give AI a problem. Try to break R<sup>2</sup>D.**
